title: Case Study 46: Electrolysis of Concentrated Hydrochloric Acid: Inert Anode Phenomena
question: Case Scenario:** Concentrated hydrochloric acid is placed in a Hoffman voltameter fitted with inert graphite (carbon) electrodes. A direct electric current is passed through the electrolyte. In the first few minutes, the volume of gas collecting in the cathode limb (hydrogen) is noticeably greater than the volume of gas collecting in the anode limb (chlorine). However, once electrolysis has proceeded for 20 minutes, the rate of gas accumulation stabilizes at an exact 1:1 volume ratio. **Investigative Question:** Why is the volume of chlorine gas collected at the anode initially less than that of hydrogen at the cathode, and what are the electrode reactions? Choose the correct option:

options.text: Chlorine molecules are destroyed by graphite electrodes to form diamond crystals.

At cathode: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂↑; at anode: 2Cl⁻ - 2e⁻ → Cl₂↑; chlorine gas is moderately soluble in water (~2 volumes of Cl₂ dissolve in 1 volume of water at room temperature), so initially evolved chlorine dissolves in the aqueous electrolyte until the solution becomes fully saturated, after which H₂ and Cl₂ collect in the theoretical 1:1 molar/volume ratio.
Hydrogen gas is denser than chlorine and compresses into a smaller volume.
The electric current breaks down carbon from the cathode into methane gas.

explanation: Electrolysis of concentrated hydrochloric acid proceeds according to: Cathode (negative): 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂↑ (reduction). Anode (positive): 2Cl⁻ - 2e⁻ → Cl₂↑ (oxidation). Overall: 2HCl(aq) → H₂(g) + Cl₂(g). According to Avogadro's law, equal moles of gases occupy equal volumes under identical conditions, predicting an exact 1:1 volume ratio. However, hydrogen is virtually insoluble in water, so all generated H₂ bubbles out immediately into the cathode limb. Chlorine gas, in contrast, is moderately soluble in aqueous solution (~2.3 L Cl₂ per 1 L water at 20°C). During the initial minutes of electrolysis, a substantial portion of the newly liberated chlorine dissolves in the surrounding aqueous solution. Only when the electrolyte becomes completely saturated with dissolved chlorine does all evolved Cl₂ gas escape into the anode tube, achieving the true 1:1 stoichiometric volume ratio.

title: Case Study 47: Comparative Acidic Strength: Degree of Ionisation of HCl vs Weak Acids
question: Case Scenario:** A physical chemistry student prepares 0.1 M aqueous solutions of three acids: Solution 1: 0.1 M Hydrochloric acid (HCl) Solution 2: 0.1 M Acetic acid (CH₃COOH) Solution 3: 0.1 M Carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) The student measures their electrical conductivities using a conductivity meter and determines their pH values using a calibrated digital pH probe. The data show: HCl has a pH of ~1.0 and high conductivity; CH₃COOH has a pH of ~2.9 and moderate conductivity; H₂CO₃ has a pH of ~3.8 and very low conductivity. **Investigative Question:** Explain why 0.1 M HCl exhibits vastly higher electrical conductivity and lower pH compared to equimolar acetic and carbonic acids. Choose the correct option:

options.text: Hydrochloric acid is a strong mineral acid that undergoes virtually 100% ionisation in water (HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻), producing a high concentration of free mobile ions ([H₃O⁺] = 0.1 M), whereas acetic acid and carbonic acid are weak acids that ionise only partially (<1.3%), leaving most solute as un-ionised molecules.
Hydrochloric acid contains sodium ions that conduct electricity faster than hydrogen.
Acetic acid neutralises its own ions into solid sugar molecules.
Carbonic acid contains no hydrogen atoms capable of carrying charge.

explanation: The strength of an acid is determined by its degree of ionisation (α) in water: 1) Strong acids: Hydrochloric acid is a strong electrolyte and a strong acid with a very large dissociation constant (Ka > 10⁶). In 0.1 M aqueous solution, its degree of ionisation is virtually 100% (α ≈ 1.0). Every single molecule dissociates: HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻. The concentration of hydronium ions is [H₃O⁺] = 0.1 M, giving pH = -log(0.1) = 1.0. 2) Weak acids: Acetic acid (CH₃COOH, Ka ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) and carbonic acid (H₂CO₃, Ka1 ≈ 4.3 × 10⁻⁷) undergo only very slight, reversible ionisation (<1.3% for 0.1 M acetic acid). Most acid remains as neutral, non-conducting covalent molecules, yielding vastly lower [H₃O⁺], higher pH, and poor electrical conductivity.

title: Case Study 48: Quantitative Carbonate Displacement: Measuring Molar Gas Volume
question: Case Scenario:** An analytical chemist reacts exactly 5.30 g of pure anhydrous sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃, molar mass = 106 g/mol) with an excess of dilute hydrochloric acid in an airtight conical flask connected to a calibrated gas syringe at Standard Temperature and Pressure (STP, 0°C and 1 atm, where 1 mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 dm³). **Investigative Question:** What volume of dry carbon dioxide gas will be collected in the gas syringe at STP? Choose the correct option:

options.text: 0.56 dm³ (560 cm³)

explanation: The stoichiometric calculation proceeds as follows: 1) Balanced chemical equation: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂↑. 2) Moles of Na₂CO₃ reacted: moles = mass / molar mass = 5.30 g / 106 g/mol = 0.050 mol. 3) Stoichiometric mole ratio: From the equation, 1 mole of Na₂CO₃ produces 1 mole of CO₂ gas. Therefore, moles of CO₂ produced = 0.050 mol. 4) Volume of CO₂ at STP: Volume = moles × molar volume at STP = 0.050 mol × 22.4 dm³/mol = 1.12 dm³ (or 1120 cm³). The gas syringe will record exactly 1.12 dm³ of carbon dioxide gas.

title: Case Study 49: Thermal Dissociation of Hydrogen Chloride Gas
question: Case Scenario:** In a high-temperature materials laboratory, pure dry hydrogen chloride gas is pumped through an alumina combustion tube and heated incrementally from 200°C to 1200°C. Gas chromatography at the outlet shows no detectable traces of free hydrogen (H₂) or chlorine (Cl₂) gas. Only when the temperature is elevated past 1500°C does a minuscule fraction (<0.3%) of the gas begin to dissociate into its constituent elements. **Investigative Question:** What thermodynamic property of hydrogen chloride explains its extraordinary thermal stability against thermal dissociation? Choose the correct option:

options.text: The H–Cl bond is an ionic bond that cannot be broken by heat.
Hydrogen chloride molecules polymerise into heat-resistant graphite fibers.
Chlorine atoms freeze into solid crystals at elevated temperatures.

The H–Cl single bond has a remarkably high covalent bond dissociation enthalpy (~431 kJ/mol), making the molecule exceptionally thermally stable, so negligible thermal dissociation (2HCl ⇌ H₂ + Cl₂ - 185 kJ) occurs below 1500°C.

explanation: Hydrogen chloride is one of the most thermally stable diatomic hydrides known. The covalent bond between hydrogen and chlorine is short (bond length ~127 pm) with significant ionic character (approx. 17%) due to the electronegativity difference (3.0 for Cl vs 2.1 for H). The bond dissociation enthalpy is an impressive 431 kJ/mol. The thermal dissociation reaction: 2HCl(g) ⇌ H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) is strongly endothermic (ΔH = +185 kJ). Thermal energy available below 1000°C is completely insufficient to break the H–Cl bond. Only at temperatures exceeding 1500°C does thermal vibration overcome this bond energy, resulting in a negligible (<0.3%) reversible dissociation.

title: Case Study 50: Environmental Safety: Acid Spill Neutralisation and Atmospheric Fogging
question: Case Scenario:** An industrial tank carrying concentrated hydrochloric acid develops a leak in a chemical depot on a humid monsoon day. Dense white suffocating 'fogs' immediately envelop the spill area. Emergency hazmat crews arrive wearing full chemical-resistant suits and immediately spread large quantities of powdered slaked lime [calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂] or crushed limestone [calcium carbonate, CaCO₃] over the liquid spill, rather than washing it down with water. **Investigative Question:** Explain why concentrated HCl produces dense fogs in humid air, and why slaked lime / limestone is used for emergency spill neutralisation. Choose the correct option:

options.text: The fog is steam caused by water freezing into ice; limestone cools the acid into snow.

HCl gas continuously escapes from concentrated acid and, being intensely hygroscopic, dissolves in water vapor in the humid atmosphere to form microscopic suspended droplets of liquid hydrochloric acid appearing as dense white fumes; slaked lime / limestone neutralises the corrosive acid into harmless calcium chloride, water, and carbon dioxide without explosive splattering (Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O).
The fog is chlorine gas; slaked lime oxidises chlorine into liquid nitrogen.
Concentrated HCl burns air into carbon smoke; limestone dissolves the smoke into oil.

explanation: 1) Atmospheric fogging: Concentrated hydrochloric acid is an aqueous solution saturated with volatile HCl gas. When exposed to ambient air, HCl gas readily escapes from the liquid surface. Because HCl has a phenomenal affinity for water (hygroscopic nature), escaping gas molecules dissolve in the water vapor present in humid air, condensing into microscopic aerosol droplets of hydrochloric acid. These suspended acid mist droplets scatter light, appearing as dense white fumes or acid fog. 2) Hazmat neutralisation: Adding water to a large concentrated acid spill causes localized boiling, spattering, and accelerates acid fogs. Hazmat crews apply basic powders such as slaked lime [Ca(OH)₂] or crushed limestone [CaCO₃]. These bases safely neutralise the acid: Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O. The products are non-volatile, non-toxic calcium chloride and neutral water, completely eliminating the hazardous acid.
